title: Watkins Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Watkins wells have a 600-foot median depth. See local yields, water levels, drilling costs, risks and permit history.
h1: Wells and Drilling Costs in Watkins, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Watkins means dealing with a deep Denver Basin well area. Among permitted wells within 5 miles, the median reported depth is 600 feet, and the middle half runs from 480 to 736 feet. Most wells are used for domestic or household water, but stock and irrigation wells are also present.

The records show generally serviceable reported yields, with a 10.0 gallon-per-minute median among wells that reported a pump yield. That does not guarantee the result on an unbuilt lot. A driller still needs to evaluate the specific parcel, aquifer target, access, casing and grout requirements, pump setting, and water-rights limits.

sections.heading: Watkins wells are commonly deep
sections.html:
Depth is the first major cost issue around Watkins. The median permitted well is 600 feet, while the middle half is 480 to 736 feet. The 90th percentile reaches 992 feet, and the deepest record is 2,047 feet. More than half of the wells in the depth mix are 600 feet or deeper.

That distribution matters when reviewing a drilling bid. A 600-foot estimate is a reasonable local planning point, but it is not a guaranteed stopping depth. Only 17% of wells are under 100 feet, and 2% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock is the reported ground model here. The Denver, Upper Arapahoe, and unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers all appear in the records, so the target formation can affect the final depth.

sections.heading: What a Watkins well may produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are stronger than the depth numbers might suggest. The median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-four percent of reported yields fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 25% report 15 gallons per minute or more.

No recorded yield in this dataset is under 1 gallon per minute, and 2% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Still, the yield figures come from only 484 wells that reported a pump yield, not every permitted well. A test result is not the same as a guaranteed long-term supply. Ask for the completion report, pumping test information, storage capacity and pump performance before assuming the well will support a house, livestock or irrigation.

sections.heading: Water levels vary across the Watkins records
sections.html:
The reported median static water level is 320 feet below the surface, with a very broad middle half from 30 to 450 feet. That range is a warning against using one neighbor's water level as a design number. Pump setting, casing depth, aquifer, land elevation and the timing of the measurement all matter.

The decade series does not show a simple dropping table in these records. The median depth to water was 360 feet in the 2010s and 280 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported median is shallower. That comparison is not proof of recovery or a basin-wide trend; it can reflect different locations, aquifers and reporting practices. A site-specific water-level check remains important when sizing the pump and pressure system.

sections.heading: A long permit history, with current activity
sections.html:
Watkins has a substantial well history. The records include 1,324 permitted wells, with 720 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued in every decade from the 1950s through the 2020s, and the newest permit year is 2025. The largest decade in the supplied history is the 2000s, with 251 permits; the 1980s and 1990s also show substantial activity.

Crandall Drilling & Pump Service, including Crandall Jr. and Howard H., appears most often with 196 records. Don Eastwood Drilling Inc., including Eastwood and Don, appears with 125, followed by Authorized, including Pe and Pg, with 83. These names describe the permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references, scope and who will perform the pump work before hiring.

sections.heading: Planning the cost of a Watkins well
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 600-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $30,000 to $42,000. A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching and electrical, models at about $36,000 to $54,000.

Those figures are planning ranges rather than a fixed quote. A deeper-than-expected hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, unusual pump requirements and electrical or trench conditions can change the total. Have the driller separate footage, casing, grout, formation testing, pump equipment, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work in writing. Also confirm what happens if the hole is low-yield or dry, since that risk needs to be addressed before drilling starts.

sections.heading: Watkins risks to check before closing
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention around Watkins. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but it is enough reason to check the property, nearby wells and available water-quality records. There are no historic mine features in the supplied map, which removes one common Colorado concern but not other sources.

Low yield and dry-hole risk still require a written drilling plan, even though the reported yield distribution is favorable. Septic setbacks, drainfield soil, driveway access, construction staging and well-to-building distances can affect where a house fits. A DWR permit is not the same as a guarantee of water quality or a guarantee that every intended use is authorized.

sections.heading: Due diligence for a Watkins lot
sections.html:
Before buying, pull the nearby completion reports and compare depth, aquifer, static water level, yield and use. Focus on wells in Watkins and nearby Aetna Estates, Aurora, Bennett and Strasburg, while remembering that conditions can change across the Denver Basin. A neighboring well can improve your estimate, but it cannot replace a parcel-specific bid.

Confirm the DWR permit status, permitted use and any augmentation-plan requirements before planning irrigation or other expanded use. Exempt household-use wells have limits, including the 35 gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and over-appropriated basins may require augmentation. For a new build, coordinate the well location with septic, the driveway, utility trenching and the house footprint before excavation. Put the drilling depth range, testing, pump equipment and dry-hole terms in the purchase and construction decisions.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Watkins, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Watkins is 600 feet. The middle half runs from 480 to 736 feet, while the 90th percentile is 992 feet. More than half of the wells are 600 feet or deeper. Actual depth depends on the parcel, the targeted Denver Basin formation and the driller's findings.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Watkins?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 600-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at $30,000 to $42,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical models at $36,000 to $54,000. Get a written bid that separates drilling, casing, equipment, trenching and electrical work.

faq.q: How much water does a Watkins well produce?
faq.a: Among 484 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-four percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. These are recorded results, not a guarantee for a new well, so request testing and completion information for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Watkins?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, there are 91 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 8 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the proposed property's water for relevant contaminants and review nearby records. A DWR permit confirms regulatory paperwork, not water quality.

faq.q: What should I check before buying land with a well near Watkins?
faq.a: Review the DWR permit, completion report, permitted use, depth, yield, static water level and maintenance history. The area includes domestic, stock and irrigation wells, so use matters. Check septic feasibility, access, utility routing and environmental records. If planning irrigation or expanded use, confirm water-rights and augmentation-plan requirements before closing.
